tiers.name: Beginner
tiers.takeaway: Develop toward the centre, aim your bishop at f7, castle early, and don't move the same piece twice without a reason.

steps.say: I've never played an opening on purpose. What should White actually do?

Three jobs: put a pawn in the centre, bring pieces out, get your king safe. It's like moving into a house. You unlock the door, carry the furniture in, then lock up. The Italian does those jobs in the plainest order there is.
Your pawn takes space in the centre and opens lines for your queen and bishop. Black does the same.
Bring out a piece that attacks something. Which move develops and hits the e5 pawn?

quiz.hint: It's a knight move, toward the centre.
quiz.hit: Knight to f3 develops and attacks e5, so Black has to spend a move answering.

steps.say: Black guards the pawn with a knight and develops too.
Now look at Black's camp. One pawn is guarded only by the king. Tap it.

quiz.hint: It's right next to the black king, on the kingside.
quiz.hit: f7. Only the king protects it, and a king is a bad defender because it can't take a guarded piece. That pawn is the target of this whole opening.

steps.say: Put your bishop on the diagonal that points at it.

quiz.hint: Your light-squared bishop on f1 can reach the a2-g8 diagonal.
quiz.hit: That's the Italian Game. About four in ten players choose it here at every level up to 2200.

steps.say: Black copies you. You play c3 so that d4 becomes possible later, and so Black's knight can't land on d4.
Black's knight hits e4, and d3 guards it with a pawn. A protected pawn is a safe pawn. This also opens your other bishop.
Both kings are safe. You've done everything the opening asked for by move 6, and the engine gives +0.11, about level.
Your rook backs up e4. Black's ...a6 was going to push your bishop with ...b5, so you step back first. It still points at f7.
Shouldn't I be attacking by now?
Not yet. Nobody has weakened anything. Keep improving your pieces until there's a real target. Rushing an attack here is how beginners lose pieces.
Lots of players do this because they fear a knight on g5. About one in six do under 1800. It stops one idea, but it doesn't develop a piece.
Black gave you a free move. Take the centre with it.

quiz.hint: Push the pawn next to your e4 pawn. If Black takes it, you take back.
quiz.hit: When your opponent spends time on a quiet move, open the game. Your pieces are ahead, so an open position favours you (+0.50).

steps.say: You take back with a piece, and you're already ahead in development.

tiers.name: Intermediate
tiers.hook: Know the two traps at this level
tiers.takeaway: A free pawn with a loose queen behind it is often bait. Before you grab or sacrifice, count who's actually attacking, and check whether Black has castled away from it.

scenes.title: The pawn you must not take

steps.say: Sometimes Black plays a weird knight move and leaves e5 hanging. Free pawn?
This is that move. It looks like a blunder, and that's the point. Here's what White does, and how White scores.

table.caption: After 3...Nd4: share of White's replies, and White's score
head: Under 1400

steps.say: So what do you play?

options.why: This is the bait. White scores under 30% after it. The next section shows the mate.
Yes. Black spent two moves on a knight that's now gone, and the recapture wrecks the pawns. The engine gives you +1.38.

steps.say: You castle and carry on. Black has a doubled-up pawn on d4 that's hard to hold and is far behind in development (+1.18).

scenes.title: What the bait does
scenes.from: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Nd4

steps.say: Black's queen attacks your knight and g2 at the same time.
You grab more: a pawn and a fork on the rook. It feels like you're winning. Black takes g2 and your rook has to step away.
The queen takes e4 with check and your bishop has to block.
Mate. Your own pieces are the walls. That Black knight has been waiting on d4 for this all along.
The engine's verdict is that even after 4...Qg5 you aren't lost if you find 5.O-O, but you'd be worse (-0.50). Nothing about the pawn was free.

scenes.title: When the knight raid works
scenes.from: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Nf6

steps.say: Now two pieces hit f7, and the king is the only defender. About a quarter to a third of players go for it. Black has to respond at once.
Black blocks the bishop with a pawn, and you take it. Now Black has a choice, and most players at your level get it wrong.

table.caption: Black's fifth move, share of games
head: Under 1400

steps.say: The natural recapture. For now the knight blocks your bishop, but f7 still has only the king guarding it.
This one is called the Fried Liver. What's the move?

quiz.hint: Take what you've been aiming at.
quiz.hit: Sacrifice the knight. The king gets dragged into the open, and White scored about 72% from here under 1800.

steps.say: Check, and the d5 knight is under attack too, by your queen and bishop. The king has to guard it.
Black's king stands on e6 in the middle of the board, and you pile on the pinned knight. The engine says about +0.9. There's still work to do, but Black has to find a lot of only-moves.

scenes.title: When the knight raid fails
scenes.from: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 d3 Nf6

steps.say: Same knight, same square. Now Black's bishop is out on c5, and that one difference changes everything.
What's Black's calm answer here? Look for the most normal move on the board. Tap the square Black's king goes to.

quiz.hint: Black has a bishop out of the way, so one special king move is available.
quiz.hit: Black castles. After 5...O-O your knight has nothing to do (-0.49). If you carry on with 6.Nxf7 Rxf7 7.Bxf7+ Kxf7, you give up two pieces for a rook and a pawn, and the engine says -2.7.

steps.say: Same plan, opposite result. Attack f7 only when Black can't simply castle out of it, which is why 4.Ng5 works against 3...Nf6, before the bishop has left f8.

tiers.name: Advanced
tiers.hook: The slow game has a plan
tiers.takeaway: Hold the d3 structure until your pieces are ready, then break with d4. When a pin or a sacrifice comes up, calculate who actually benefits, because the slow Italian rewards patience over tactics.

scenes.title: Solid moves that give you the centre
scenes.from: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 c3

steps.say: I reach move ten fine, and then I have no idea what I'm trying to do.
Start by noticing how much Black's move order matters. After c3 you threaten d4, and the best reply is to counterattack e4 with ...Nf6.
A natural, solid move. About a third of players up to 2200 choose it. It looks fine, and it hands you the centre.
Punish it.

quiz.hint: You've been preparing this push since move 4.
quiz.hit: Without a knight on f6 hitting e4, you can just take the centre (+0.55, against +0.17 after 4...Nf6). Black's bishop has to drop back.

steps.say: You have two pawns side by side in the centre, and Black has no pawn there at all. Your next moves come easily.

scenes.title: Black's best reply to 6.e5
scenes.from: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 c3 Nf6 d4 exd4

steps.say: Say you choose the sharp 5.d4 instead of 5.d3. Now the same question flips: can Black find the answer?
Your pawn hits the knight. Look at how differently players handle it.

table.caption: Black's sixth move after 6.e5, share of games
head: Under 1400

steps.say: Knight moves feel obvious, and they're bad: +1.17 after 6...Ng4 and +1.61 after 6...Ne4. The counter-punch 6...d5 is level (+0.05). It's worth playing 5.d4 at club level because so few people find it.
Against the right reply, you pin the knight and win your pawn back. It's a normal game with a small edge (+0.21). So 5.d4 risks very little.

scenes.title: The plan: knight to g3, then d4
scenes.from: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 c3 Nf6 d3 d6 O-O O-O Re1 a6 Bb3 Ba7

steps.say: Back to the slow line. Black's bishop has dropped to a7 so it can't be chased. Before anything else, deal with a piece that wants to come out.
Which pawn move stops ...Bg4 and ...Ng4 for good?

quiz.hint: Control g4 with a pawn from the h-file.
quiz.hit: A small move that matters. A pin on your f3 knight would slow every plan you have, and now it can't happen.

steps.say: The knight takes the long road, through d2 and f1, heading for g3. From there it eyes f5 and h5, where it bothers Black's king.
Black offers a bishop trade. You keep yours by stepping to c2, because it supports your central break later. It still looks at the kingside.
Black takes the centre first. This is fine, and the engine calls it level. Now you know what you're playing for: e4 and d4 against e5 and d5, with your pieces already in place.

scenes.title: The sacrifice that looks strong
scenes.from: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 c3 Nf6 d3 d6 O-O O-O

steps.say: You pin the knight. Black kicks the bishop and throws the g-pawn forward, exposing the king.
Black's kingside looks wrecked. Do you sacrifice on g5?

options.why: It looks crushing and it doesn't work. After 9...hxg5 10.Bxg5 you have two pawns and a pin for the knight, and Black is better (-1.08 after 10...Kg7). The king walks to safety on g7 and then the rook arrives on h8.
Right. It's not exciting, and it holds a small edge (+0.13). Black's pawns on g5 and h6 are now permanent weaknesses around the king, and you've given up nothing.

steps.say: The bishop stays alive and pressures e5. Calculate the sacrifice every time, because a tempo either way can flip it. Here, patience is the better attack.

tiers.name: Master
tiers.hook: Keep the pieces on, or open it up
tiers.takeaway: Slow Italian keeps every piece on and asks for a better plan. Evans gives a pawn for a storm. Pick by the opponent in front of you.

scenes.title: The move order at the top

steps.say: I know the slow Italian, and everyone I play knows it too. How do I get anything from it?
First see what's changed. As ratings rise, Black plays 3...Nf6 more, and White answers more quietly.

table.caption: Share of games at each step
head: Under 1400

steps.say: Black's bishop doesn't go to c5. It stays back on e7, where it can't be hit by d4 or b4, and it keeps ...d5 ready.
Both castle. Both sides are still fully loaded.
What's the useful waiting move that stops ...b5 and gains queenside room?

quiz.hint: It takes the b5 square away with a rook's pawn.
quiz.hit: A little space move, and your bishop can stay on c4 now that ...b5 won't come easily.

steps.say: Black hits the centre, and it's +0.15. Nothing is forced, and both sides still have every minor piece. That's the point of this opening at the top: a long game where the better plan wins.

scenes.title: The Evans: a pawn for a storm
scenes.from: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5

steps.say: If you'd rather have a fight than a long squeeze, this is the most direct choice in the whole Italian.
You offer a pawn to pull the bishop off c5 and gain time. It's played more as ratings rise: 3%, 6%, 8%, 11% across the bands.
The bishop has to move again, and d4 is coming with tempo.
A pawn down, with a huge centre and open lines. The engine gives -0.03, so your compensation is complete.
Black chooses the calm defence, and your queen lines up on f7 and b7 together. Black's correct answer is 7...Qd7.
That's ugly, but it holds. The queen blocks the c8 bishop. White has real play, and Black has to prove the extra pawn. At the board that's hard to do.

scenes.title: When you castle first: 5.d4
scenes.from: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 O-O Nf6

steps.say: You offer a pawn for fast development. Here the bands disagree sharply about how to reply.
This is Black's choice and worth knowing from your side.

steps.say: The engine gives +0.26 after 5...exd4, where you continue 6.e5 and it scored about 68% in the two lower bands. It gives -0.24 after 5...Bxd4. So this gambit is a good practical try, and an informed opponent can hand it back. Don't play it against someone who has prepared.
